stt: Ask YC: What's the most inspiring sci-fi book you've read?
x:
depends on the subgenre :)

Superhuman:
Slan by A.E. Van Vogt
More Than Human by Theodore STurgeon
Odd John by Olaf Stapledon

Post Apocalyptic:
The Day of The Triffids by John Whyndham
Earth Abides by George R. Stewart
A Canticle for Lebowitz by...don't remember

Space Opera/Adventure:
any of The Culture novels by Iain M. Banks
The Reality Dysfunction series by ...don't remember
Hyperion series by Dan Simmons
To Your Scattered Bodies Go by Philip Jose Farmer

Dystopian:
We by Yevgeny Zamyatin <---highly overlooked, predates 1984 and Brave New World

But the Absolute Best would be anything by:
Stanislaw Lem (Cyberiad, Futurological Congress, Solaris)
Alfred Bester (The STars my Destination, The Demolished Man)
or Samuel R. Delany (Babel-17, Dhalgren, Trtion, Nova)
oh and Roger Zelazny's Lord of Light and This Immortal are both great.

Some of Philip K. Dick's stuff is great, but everyone recommends him. :)

almost forgot John Brunner, check out Steel Beach, The Sheep Look Up, and Stand on Zanzibar.

stt: Ask HN: What are you reading?
x:
Recently I have begun reading more than one book at a time, which I have never done before.

I'm not stellar at this yet, trying to juggle three turns into progressing two fairly quickly with the third much slower...

Clive Barker, Books of Blood - Currently in volume three. I've always found horror to require, like fantasy, a concentrated effort on my part as a reader to sustain suspension of disbelief. But these are great fun even if that's difficult sometimes.

Yevgeny Zamyatin, We - With sci-fi for whatever reason I do not suffer from the suspension-of-disbelief problem, the worldbuilding is much easier to immerse myself in. (Before this I was reading Roadside Picnic which was extremely good)

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, The Gulag Archipelago - The slow one, still very interesting, nonfiction is uncommon for me
